slides.text: Nobody reads the classifieds in a dying county newspaper except the person who typesets them. Every Tuesday morning for three years, a frail woman in a lavender cardigan has walked into our front office, paid forty-two dollars in crisp two-dollar bills, and submitted a three-line 'In Memoriam' notice for a different name and city: 'Beloved brother, gone to rest where the pines meet the water.'

Last month, boredom got the better of me. I cross-referenced the names and cities from her Tuesday notices in a national public-records database. Every single person she mourned was very much alive on the Tuesday the paper went to press—and every single one of them died of an 'accidental household fall' in that exact city on the following Friday.

Digging deeper, I realized all thirty-six men had been acquitted of violent crimes in the 1980s where the lead prosecutor was a woman who disappeared in 1991. Five minutes ago, the bell above my office door chimed. The woman in the lavender cardigan smiled warmly, placed forty-two dollars on my desk, and slid over a handwritten slip for tomorrow's edition. The name on the paper was mine.
